description: No source shows Bohannan's campaign platform addressing data centers, AI infrastructure guardrails, or corporate development scrutiny in this context. Her official campaign priorities page (checked in full across multiple research passes) contains no mention of data centers. This is a fabricated policy position presented as her own stated stance.

inaccurate_statement: Opponents have framed Bohannan as a 'multimillionaire liberal' whose proposed policies would increase economic burdens, rather than lower taxes, for local Iowa families
description: No record exists of Bohannan being labeled specifically a 'multimillionaire liberal' by opponents. Attack coverage has referred to her as a 'radical progressive' (Miller-Meeks's own characterization) and has scrutinized her stock holdings and home ownership, but the specific 'multimillionaire liberal' framing does not match documented attack lines against her.

inaccurate_statement: Critics have accused Bohannan of 'evaluating early American history through frames that emphasize the preservation of slavery'
description: No record exists of this specific characterization or attack line against Bohannan. Her documented controversies include the 2021 'backwater' quote about a transgender athletes bill and a separate 'backwards state' comment about DEI training restrictions, plus scrutiny of her DEI committee work promoting donations to bail funds. There is no documented basis for this specific claim about her framing early American history around slavery preservation; it appears to be an invented elaboration not grounded in any known controversy.

inaccurate_statement: A formal complaint was filed with the Office of Congressional Ethics alleging Miller-Meeks committed 'election misconduct and voter fraud'
description: A residency-related ethics complaint and a separate county-board residency challenge were real and documented, but no official body — the Scott County board, the Office of Congressional Ethics, or any court — has found that Miller-Meeks committed voter fraud or election misconduct. The Scott County board actually accepted and counted her 2024 ballot, and OCE did not pursue the complaint further. Characterizing the complaint's substance as an adjudicated or even squarely-alleged 'voter fraud' finding overstates what is actually a real but unresolved and disputed controversy.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks maintained her primary residence in Ottumwa while registering to vote using a Davenport (Scott County) address, and this Davenport address is the one at issue in the ethics complaint
description: The documented registration timeline shows she first registered at a state senator's home in LeClaire (Scott County) in October 2022, then registered at a Davenport apartment in 2024 (voting there that November) — and the residency challenge/ethics complaint in fall 2024 concerned that period. She later re-registered in December 2025 at her Ottumwa home, which is outside IA-01. The response conflates and compresses this timeline, describing the Davenport address as being used concurrently with a claimed Ottumwa 'primary residence' at the time of the complaint, when the actual chronology involves sequential registration changes across different addresses and years.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's office points to her being out across the district's 20 counties as evidence of accessibility.
description: Miller-Meeks completed a 20-county in-person tour, but the dossier describes this as a broader factual point rather than something specifically framed by her office as a defense against town-hall criticism; this detail is closely aligned with the documented record (a 20-county tour did occur), so any discrepancy here is negligible and largely accurate in substance.

inaccurate_statement: Christina Bohannan centers her campaign platform on working across the aisle and reducing partisan bickering.
description: Bohannan's official 2026 campaign platform centers on lowering costs, health care, ethics reform, education, family farms, and reproductive freedom, framed largely through sharp partisan contrasts with her opponent's voting record and corporate donations. 'Extreme partisanship' is mentioned only briefly as one of several problems alongside 'the corrupting influence of money and special interests,' and only one bipartisan bill from her state legislative record is cited. Her messaging is dominated by economic populism and pointed attacks on her opponent's record rather than a defining 'working across the aisle' theme.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has voted to override certain presidential vetoes as an example of bipartisan independence.
description: There is no record in the available material of Miller-Meeks voting to override a presidential veto during her time in Congress (2023–present, under Democratic and then Republican presidents). No such veto-override vote is documented in her legislative record, and this appears to be an invented or unsupported specific example of bipartisanship attributed to her.

inaccurate_statement: EMILY's List endorsed her nomination to help flip the House [attributed to Miller-Meeks]
description: EMILY's List is a Democratic organization that supports pro-choice Democratic women; it has endorsed Christina Bohannan (first endorsed in 2022, renewed for 2026), not Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican. The response's structure attributes this endorsement to Miller-Meeks, which reverses the actual endorsement and misleads readers about which candidate has this support.

inaccurate_statement: Reproductive Freedom for All, Everytown for Gun Safety, and the League of Conservation Voters endorsed her [attributed to Miller-Meeks]
description: Reproductive Freedom for All, Everytown for Gun Safety Action Fund, and LCV Action Fund are all progressive/Democratic-aligned advocacy organizations that have endorsed Christina Bohannan, not Mariannette Miller-Meeks. Miller-Meeks is pro-life and has a Republican voting record on guns and environmental regulation, making endorsements from these groups implausible and contrary to the documented record, which shows these groups backing Bohannan instead.

inaccurate_statement: EMILY's List endorsed Bohannan as a key 'red-to-blue' candidate
description: The 'Red to Blue' program is run by the DCCC, not EMILY's List. EMILY's List has its own separate, longstanding endorsement of Bohannan (since 2022) unrelated to the DCCC's Red to Blue program, so attributing 'red-to-blue' status to EMILY's List conflates two distinct organizations' endorsements.

inaccurate_statement: New Democrat Coalition Action Fund named Bohannan to their initial 2026 midterm endorsement slate
description: No record exists of a New Democrat Coalition Action Fund endorsement of Christina Bohannan. This is a specific, named organizational endorsement not found in the available research, though it is a narrow, peripheral detail that does not change the overall accurate picture that Bohannan has received numerous real endorsements.

inaccurate_statement: Donald Trump endorsed Miller-Meeks, highlighting her background as a medical doctor and U.S. Army veteran
description: Trump's endorsement of Miller-Meeks (a 'Complete and Total Endorsement' issued in November 2025) is well documented, but no source ties his endorsement statement to specifically highlighting her medical or military background as the stated rationale. This specific framing detail appears to be an embellishment not grounded in the actual endorsement announcement.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan raised approximately $4.5 million specifically from individual contributors.
description: According to FEC data for the filing period ending June 30, 2026, Bohannan's individual contributions totaled $5,648,339.98, not approximately $4.5 million — the actual figure is over $1 million higher than stated.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's campaign has heavily emphasized grassroots and individual small-dollar contributions from supporters looking to flip the district.
description: FEC-based reporting on Bohannan's donor breakdown found that large individual contributions, not small-dollar donations, made up the largest share of her individual fundraising, which cuts against a characterization emphasizing small-dollar/grassroots giving as her primary funding driver.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks raised millions through individual donors, alongside support from political action committees and party committees.
description: Per FEC filings for the period ending June 30, 2026, Miller-Meeks's individual contributions totaled $2,945,343.16, which is less than her PAC/committee contributions of $2,416,206.95 combined with transfers from other authorized committees of $1,686,037.07 — while individuals are still her largest single category, the framing obscures that PAC money made up a substantially larger share of her fundraising than is typical for a campaign primarily described as individual-donor-driven, and this doesn't undermine the overall accurate point that she does raise from a mix of individuals, PACs, and committees.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has brought in approximately $4.5 million from individual contributors
description: Per FEC data for the filing period ending June 30, 2026, Christina Bohannan's total individual contributions were $5,648,339.98, not approximately $4.5 million.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has raised roughly $2.5 million directly from individual donors
description: Per FEC data for the filing period ending June 30, 2026, Miller-Meeks's individual contributions totaled $2,945,343.16, closer to $2.9 million than $2.5 million, though this is a relatively narrow numerical discrepancy.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan focuses on expanding Medicaid while opposing cuts to healthcare programs.
description: Bohannan's documented healthcare platform centers on a Medicare buy-in at any age, expanding Medicare to vision/dental/hearing, capping insulin costs, and reversing Medicaid cuts (i.e., opposing cuts to existing Medicaid, not proposing to expand it as a distinct policy). There is no record of her proposing to actually expand Medicaid eligibility or benefits as a named platform item; her documented position is reversing Medicaid cuts to prevent rural hospital closures, which is a narrower claim than 'expanding Medicaid.'

inaccurate_statement: Both candidates face each other after extremely close past results
description: Only the 2024 matchup between Bohannan and Miller-Meeks was extremely close, decided by just 799 votes after a recount. Their 2022 matchup was not close at all — Miller-Meeks won comfortably by about 7 points (53%-47%). Describing the 'past results' collectively as 'extremely close' mischaracterizes the 2022 race.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is seeking her fourth term
description: Miller-Meeks is the sitting incumbent seeking a third consecutive term representing Iowa's 1st Congressional District specifically (having won the seat in 2022 and 2024, after winning the old, differently-numbered IA-02 in 2020). Describing this as her 'fourth term' without clarifying that one of those terms was in a different, pre-redistricting district could be read as a term-count of the current seat, which would be inaccurate — she would be starting her third term representing IA-01 if she wins in 2026, though it would be her fourth term in the U.S. House overall.

inaccurate_statement: Both candidates face each other after extremely close past results
description: Only the 2024 matchup between Bohannan and Miller-Meeks was extremely close, decided by just 799 votes after a recount. Their 2022 matchup was not close at all — Miller-Meeks won comfortably by about 7 points (53%-47%). Describing the 'past results' collectively as 'extremely close' mischaracterizes the 2022 race.

inaccurate_statement: Critics point to her votes against measures like the Consumer Fuel Price Gouging Prevention Act
description: No record in the available material confirms a Miller-Meeks vote against a 'Consumer Fuel Price Gouging Prevention Act,' though she has been criticized for opposing similar corporate-accountability/price-gouging measures in general terms. This specific bill and vote could not be verified against her documented voting record.

inaccurate_statement: Critics contend that her support for major Republican tax packages, such as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, disproportionately benefits the top 1% of earners and large corporations while threatening reductions in social safety programs
description: This is presented as a specific critics' claim about distributional impact on 'the top 1% of earners' specifically. The dossier documents that OBBBA contains Medicaid work-requirement provisions and cuts that critics say hurt low-income Iowans, and that KFF estimates ~110,000 more Iowans uninsured by 2034, but does not document a specific '1%' distributional claim being made by her critics in this race. This specific framing is not clearly grounded in the documented criticism and should be treated with caution, though the general thrust that critics call the bill corporate/wealthy-favoring is otherwise supported.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks was fined $500 by the House Ethics Committee for violating federal House floor mask mandates
description: She was fined $500 by the House Sergeant at Arms for going maskless on the House floor, and the House Ethics Committee later published/documented this fine rather than being the body that levied it. This is a narrow procedural distinction that doesn't change the core fact that she was fined and did violate the mask mandate.

inaccurate_statement: Multiple complaints were filed with the House Committee on Ethics alleging she violated Iowa voting laws over her residency
description: The residency/voting complaint was filed with the federal Office of Congressional Ethics (OCE), and a separate residency challenge was filed with the Scott County board of supervisors — not the House Committee on Ethics directly. The Scott County board accepted and counted her ballot, and no official body found she broke the law.

inaccurate_statement: The 2020 financial disclosure complaint claimed she failed to report at least $25,000 from her prior salary as an Iowa State Senator, in addition to the $35,000 in pension/Great River Health Systems income
description: The dossier's documented complaint describes roughly $34,646-$35,000 in total unreported/misstated income encompassing her state pension, Great River Health Systems payments, and her state senate salary combined — not an additional separate $25,000 salary figure on top of the $35,000. The response appears to double-count or misstate the breakdown of the alleged unreported income.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's legal team faced pushback for objecting to a federal House review of her own election while she simultaneously signed onto generic Republican letters calling for a broader investigation into 2020 election irregularities, and her name was later removed from that letter
description: Contemporaneous reporting indicates Miller-Meeks's campaign stated she never signed or agreed to be included on the letter urging investigation of 2020 election irregularities; her name was reportedly added in error by a colleague's staff and then removed, rather than her having signed it and then had it retracted.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks amended her financial disclosure to officially disclose between $880,000 and $2.6 million in previously unlisted retirement assets and salaries
description: The documented ethics complaint concerned roughly $34,000-$80,000 in omitted income and assets (state pension, state senate salary, Great River Health Systems income, and retirement account assets), not a figure in the hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. No source in the available record supports an $880,000 to $2.6 million disclosed amount.

inaccurate_statement: The hoax veterans'-benefits story Miller-Meeks shared forced a regional VA hospital to issue an emergency alert clarifying that benefits were safe
description: While it is well documented that Miller-Meeks shared this satirical story and it caused concern among veterans, no source confirms that a regional VA hospital issued an emergency alert in response; this appears to be an embellishment added to an otherwise accurate underlying story.

inaccurate_statement: The complaint about her voter registration/residency was filed with the Office of Congressional Ethics regarding Scott County while her Ottumwa home is outside her district
description: The documented residency controversy involves Miller-Meeks registering at a LeClaire address in October 2022, then a Davenport apartment in 2024 (both in Scott County, within IA-01), while continuing to claim an Ottumwa property-tax homestead credit. A Bettendorf resident (not the OCE itself) filed both a residency challenge with the Scott County board and a separate OCE complaint in fall 2024. The Scott County board accepted and counted her 2024 ballot, and the OCE did not pursue the complaint further. The response's framing generally aligns with this but omits that no official body found wrongdoing, and conflates some details of the challenge process, though the core facts (Ottumwa residence outside the district, a complaint filed, dismissal by her campaign as frivolous) are substantively accurate.

inaccurate_statement: At a separate public forum, Miller-Meeks denied ever voting in favor of Donald Trump's tariff policies, and attendees booed her after being shown her voting record
description: No record exists of this specific incident in which Miller-Meeks denied voting for tariff policies at a public forum and was then confronted with her voting record, leading to booing. The documented town-hall controversy involves her Keosauqua town hall over healthcare, Medicaid, and federal spending, and separate voting-record facts show she voted multiple times to block ending tariff emergencies. No source describes this specific tariff-denial-and-booing incident, so it is unverifiable as described and inconsistent with the documented town-hall record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's campaign mistakenly paid her son, Jonathan Miller-Meeks, $3,500 from her campaign account for "consulting," and the money was returned 22 days later with an amended FEC report
description: No record in available material corroborates this specific claim about a $3,500 payment to a son named Jonathan Miller-Meeks for consulting, a 22-day return period, or an amended FEC filing describing this specific error. While the dossier does note general scrutiny over campaign expenditures including payments to family members for consulting work, this specific dollar figure, family member name, and timeline could not be verified and appear to be a fabricated or invented detail layered onto a real but more general concern.

inaccurate_statement: Political opponents criticize her for voting against certain budget amendments meant to protect Medicaid funding.
description: Miller-Meeks's documented Medicaid-related vote of significance is her yes vote on the 2025 reconciliation bill (OBBBA), which contained Medicaid work-requirement provisions and cuts, not a vote against a specific budget amendment framed as 'protecting Medicaid funding.' The response's vague framing of 'certain budget amendments' does not match the specific, well-documented vote record, making this an imprecise characterization rather than a clearly sourced claim.

inaccurate_statement: Research groups warn that if these financial credits expire, monthly insurance bills could double or increase significantly for thousands of families in Iowa and across the nation.
description: KFF has estimated that the combined expiration of enhanced ACA subsidies and Medicaid cuts could result in roughly 110,000 more uninsured Iowans, and health policy organizations have warned premiums could rise substantially or roughly double for many marketplace enrollees if subsidies expire — this is a real, nonpartisan estimate, so the claim is broadly consistent with available reporting. It is included here only to note that Miller-Meeks's office has publicly disputed the causal framing tying local provider/cost problems specifically to her votes, a nuance the response omits, though this alone is not enough to make the statement inaccurate.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan supports expanding Medicare to cover home health costs for family caregivers
description: Bohannan's documented Medicare expansion proposal centers on a Medicare buy-in at any age plus adding dental, hearing, and vision coverage; her platform materials do not establish home health costs for family caregivers as part of this plan, and other research found this specific benefit was not part of her described Medicare platform.

inaccurate_statement: Medicare Expansion: Expand Medicare coverage to include vision, dental, hearing care, and home health costs for family caregivers.
description: Bohannan's documented Medicare expansion proposal centers on adding dental, hearing, and vision coverage alongside a Medicare buy-in option at any age. Home health costs for family caregivers is a separate proposal she has made regarding caregiver support, but it is not consistently documented as part of her core 'Medicare expansion' plank in the same way vision, dental, and hearing coverage are, and combining them without distinction slightly overstates the specificity of her core, most-cited Medicare platform.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's healthcare platform includes expanding Medicare to add coverage for dental, vision, hearing, and home health care
description: Bohannan's documented Medicare expansion proposal adds dental, hearing, and vision coverage along with a Medicare buy-in option, but does not include home health care as part of this specific plan. Multiple sources confirm her stated Medicare expansion covers dental, hearing, and vision only, not home health services.

inaccurate_statement: She served as a private [in the military]
description: There is no record in her biography of her serving as an enlisted private; she joined the Army Medical Department and her documented military roles are nursing and medical officer positions, not a description of starting as a private specifically noted anywhere in her biography.

inaccurate_statement: State Health Director: Appointed by Iowa Governor Terry Branstad as the Director of the Iowa Department of Public Health, serving from 2010 to 2014
description: Miller-Meeks served as Iowa Department of Public Health Director from 2010 to 2013, not through 2014 — she resigned in 2013 to run for Congress.

inaccurate_statement: Served as president of the Iowa Academy of Ophthalmology and president of the medical staff at Ottumwa Regional Health Center
description: Miller-Meeks's documented leadership roles are as the first female president of the Iowa Medical Society and the first woman in 20 years on the University of Iowa ophthalmology faculty; there is no record of her serving as president of the Iowa Academy of Ophthalmology or president of the medical staff at Ottumwa Regional Health Center.

inaccurate_statement: Assumed office in January 2021 representing Iowa's 1st Congressional District
description: Miller-Meeks was first elected to Congress in November 2020 and took office in January 2021 representing Iowa's 2nd Congressional District under the pre-2022 redistricting map, not the 1st District; she began representing the 1st District only in January 2023 after redistricting.

inaccurate_statement: Enlisted in the U.S. Army at age 18
description: No record supports the specific claim that she enlisted at age 18; her documented Army service ran from 1974 to 1982 (Army Medical Department, retired Lieutenant Colonel), followed by Army Reserve service from 1983 to 2000, but no source specifies her enlistment age.

inaccurate_statement: Introduced bills like the Supporting Children's Mental Health Care Access Act to expand behavioral health resources
description: No evidence in the available record ties Miller-Meeks to a bill titled the 'Supporting Children's Mental Health Care Access Act.' Her documented children's mental health/AI-safety work includes the Conversational AI Services Act and other named bills, but this specific title does not appear in her sponsored or co-sponsored legislation record.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan criticized Miller-Meeks for relying heavily on out-of-state and corporate donations, contrasting it with her own grassroots support coming from hardworking Iowa families.
description: While it is accurate that Bohannan's fundraising draws a somewhat higher share from within Iowa compared to Miller-Meeks, and that Miller-Meeks accepts corporate PAC money while Bohannan does not, there is no confirmed direct Bohannan quote or statement specifically framing this as an attack contrasting 'out-of-state and corporate donations' with 'hardworking Iowa families' grassroots support. This narrative is plausible given both candidates' documented fundraising patterns, but the specific framing and attribution as a direct Bohannan criticism could not be verified against her documented statements.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan opposed carbon capture pipeline projects that rely on eminent domain to take private land from Iowa landowners, whereas she criticized Miller-Meeks' stance on the projects.
description: Bohannan's opposition to eminent domain for carbon capture pipelines is documented and accurate. However, Miller-Meeks's own position on these pipelines is that she has expressed support for carbon capture projects to aid the ethanol industry while also opposing the use of eminent domain for them -- meaning the two candidates' stated positions on eminent domain specifically are not clearly opposed to the degree the claim implies. Framing this as a clear-cut criticism of Miller-Meeks's 'stance on the projects' overstates the documented contrast between the two candidates' actual positions.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan criticizes Miller-Meeks for voting against the bipartisan infrastructure law while noting Miller-Meeks has taken credit for parts of it
description: This is broadly accurate: Bohannan has criticized Miller-Meeks for voting against the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law and pointed out that Miller-Meeks has touted funding from bills she opposed. This is well-documented in both dossiers, so it is not an error; it is included here only because it overlaps with the accurate list, and is otherwise fine as stated.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan points out that Miller-Meeks voted against the PACT Act (burn pit legislation for veterans)
description: Neither dossier documents any Bohannan criticism of Miller-Meeks specifically regarding a vote against the PACT Act. The Bohannan dossier's catalog of her criticisms of Miller-Meeks does not mention veterans' burn pit legislation, and Miller-Meeks's own dossier records no vote against the PACT Act; it instead notes her criticism of Miller-Meeks for opposing burn pit reform legislation as a separate, unconfirmed thread found only in third-party sweep notes ('Bohannan criticized Miller-Meeks for opposing burn pit reform legislation intended to provide healthcare to toxic-exposed veterans' appears in the Miller-Meeks live-search sweep as accurate, but there it refers to a different, unspecified burn pit bill, not confirmed to be the PACT Act specifically). Given the lack of clear substantiation tying this specific claim (PACT Act vote) to a documented Bohannan attack line, this is a minor, likely overstated/conflated claim.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks defeated Bohannan in closely contested races (plural) for Iowa's 1st Congressional District
description: Only one of the two prior Miller-Meeks vs. Bohannan races was closely contested. The 2022 race was a comfortable Miller-Meeks win by about 7 points (53%-47%), not close; only the 2024 race was genuinely razor-thin, decided by 799 votes after a recount. Describing both races as 'closely contested' misstates the 2022 result.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has directed federal funds toward local water and wastewater system capacity enhancements to manage heavy rain overflows
description: Miller-Meeks's confirmed water infrastructure funding is specific and itemized (the $3 million Davenport Water Pollution Control Plant project, plus earlier Mediapolis wastewater funding), not a broadly stated 'regional grants' program framed around managing heavy rain overflows generally. Presenting this as a distinct, named policy category beyond the specific documented projects overstates and generalizes what is actually a narrower, itemized funding record.

inaccurate_statement: She worked to restore critical state and federal funding for the Iowa Cancer Registry to accurately track and understand the state's cancer trends.
description: No evidence supports this claim. The Iowa Cancer Registry's funding is a state-level matter, and recent threats to its funding have come from federal budget cuts to the CDC generally, not from any documented effort by Miller-Meeks to restore funding to it specifically. Her documented cancer-related legislative record consists of federal bills on screening and early detection (the EARLY Act reauthorization, Medicare coverage for multi-cancer early detection tests), not action tied to the Iowa Cancer Registry's funding.

inaccurate_statement: She has held discussions with National Institutes of Health (NIH) leadership to advocate for continued federal research funding into the root causes and treatments of cancer.
description: No documented evidence supports a specific claim that Miller-Meeks held discussions with NIH leadership on this topic; this appears to be an unverified or invented detail rather than a sourced fact about her record.

inaccurate_statement: Championed provisions to establish Medicare coverage for MCED blood tests starting in 2029
description: Multiple sources, including her own congressional press release and independent coverage, confirm that the Medicare coverage for FDA-approved multi-cancer early-detection tests established under legislation she co-sponsored begins in 2028, not 2029.

inaccurate_statement: Worked to restore critical funding for the Iowa Cancer Registry so researchers can accurately track cancer rates and identify local trends
description: No evidence supports this claim. The Iowa Cancer Registry's funding is a state and federal (CDC) matter, and no press releases, news coverage, or legislative record ties Miller-Meeks to any effort to restore or protect its funding specifically. Her documented cancer-related record centers on other measures, such as the multi-cancer early-detection Medicare coverage bill and the EARLY Act reauthorization, not the Registry's funding or data infrastructure.

inaccurate_statement: Consulted with National Institutes of Health (NIH) leadership to ensure ongoing federal support and funding for medical research into cancer causes and treatments
description: No source substantiates that Miller-Meeks held discussions or consultations with NIH leadership specifically about cancer research funding. Her documented cancer-related legislative record involves sponsoring screening and early-detection bills (the multi-cancer early-detection Medicare coverage act, the EARLY Act reauthorization) rather than any confirmed direct engagement with NIH leadership on research funding.

inaccurate_statement: Medicare coverage for FDA-approved MCED screening tests starts in 2029.
description: Multiple sources, including Miller-Meeks's own press releases and the bill text, confirm Medicare coverage for FDA-approved multi-cancer early detection tests under the Nancy Gardner Sewell Medicare Multi-Cancer Early Detection Screening Coverage Act begins in 2028, not 2029.

inaccurate_statement: Secured $500,000 for the Oskaloosa SAFECity Initiative including school panic button systems under Alyssa's Law
description: Miller-Meeks did secure $500,000 in federal funding for Oskaloosa's SAFECity Initiative, which does include school safety panic buttons among other technologies. However, there is no evidence that this funding is specifically tied to or authorized under 'Alyssa's Law' — the federal ALYSSA Act was sponsored by Rep. Josh Gottheimer and has not passed, and Iowa has not enacted a state-level Alyssa's Law. Framing the panic-button funding as being 'under Alyssa's Law' misattributes the legal basis for this initiative.

inaccurate_statement: Co-sponsored the Defund Cities that Defund the Police Act to withhold federal grants from unsupportive municipalities
description: No record exists in the available material confirming that Miller-Meeks co-sponsored a bill called the 'Defund Cities that Defund the Police Act.' This specific legislative claim could not be substantiated, and her documented public-safety record centers on other measures (SAFECity funding, COPS program support, body cameras, Laken Riley Act, HALT Fentanyl Act) rather than this named bill.

inaccurate_statement: Directed funds toward school safety panic buttons and a Distributed Antenna System under Alyssa's Law to directly connect schools to law enforcement.
description: There is no federal 'Alyssa's Law' legislation that Miller-Meeks sponsored, cosponsored, or voted on; the actual federal ALYSSA Act was introduced by a different member of Congress and never became law, and Iowa has not enacted a state-level Alyssa's Law either. The school safety panic buttons Miller-Meeks helped fund were part of the broader Oskaloosa SAFECity Initiative appropriation, not tied to any law by that name.

inaccurate_statement: Supported funding under Alyssa's Law to install direct school panic buttons connecting facilities straight to law enforcement
description: The federal Alyssa's Law (ALYSSA Act) was sponsored by Rep. Josh Gottheimer, not Miller-Meeks, and Miller-Meeks is not a cosponsor of either version introduced in Congress; Iowa also has no state-level Alyssa's Law. Miller-Meeks did vote for a broader Oskaloosa public-safety appropriations package that included funding for school safety panic buttons among many other technologies, but this was not tied to or framed as 'Alyssa's Law' funding, making the specific attribution incorrect even though the underlying panic-button funding fact has some basis.

inaccurate_statement: She leads a bipartisan effort to require regular federal reporting on fertilizer pricing
description: The bipartisan Fertilizer Transparency Act, requiring regular federal reporting on fertilizer pricing, was introduced and led by Reps. Dusty Johnson (R-SD) and Brad Finstad (R-MN), with a Senate companion led by Sens. Thune and Klobuchar. Miller-Meeks is one of several cosponsors, not the lead of this effort.

inaccurate_statement: Supported the Cattle Contract Library Act to challenge anti-competitive practices by large corporations and protect small cattle farmers
description: There is no record indicating Miller-Meeks specifically sponsored or led the Cattle Contract Library Act; her documented antitrust-related agriculture legislation centers on the Meat Packing Special Investigator Act. While she may have supported this bill in some capacity, no specific sourcing ties her to it as a named backer, making this an unverified attribution rather than a confirmed fact.

inaccurate_statement: Co-led federal initiatives to defend the stepped-up basis tax provision, preventing farm families from being hit with capital gains taxes when inheriting land
description: Miller-Meeks does support and has publicly advocated for preserving the stepped-up basis tax rule, but available research found no evidence she 'co-led' a specific federal initiative on this provision as a discrete, named effort distinct from her broader tax/estate-tax advocacy; this appears to overstate the specificity of a real but more general position.

inaccurate_statement: The suspension of Moroccan phosphate fertilizer duties cuts farm expenses by an estimated $1.82 billion annually nationwide
description: No source in available research corroborates this specific $1.82 billion nationwide savings figure tied to the Moroccan phosphate fertilizer duty suspension; while Miller-Meeks's fertilizer-cost-relief bill is real and confirmed, this precise dollar estimate could not be verified against any documented source.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks pushes the Treasury Department to provide clear, Midwest-friendly rules for the Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production Credit to incentivize clean energy infrastructure and drive local financial investment
description: While Miller-Meeks is documented as pressuring the Treasury to finalize favorable 45Z clean fuel production tax credit rules for sustainable aviation fuels and ethanol processing, the framing describing this as generally incentivizing 'clean energy infrastructure' broadly (rather than specifically biofuels/SAF) is an imprecise characterization not fully matching the documented, narrower scope of her advocacy.

inaccurate_statement: She cosponsored the Agent Raul Gonzalez Officer Safety Act to make fleeing from law enforcement a federal crime.
description: Miller-Meeks's record includes support for legislation related to officer safety and penalizing fleeing from law enforcement at the border, and the dossier lists votes for the 'Agent Raul Gonzalez Officer Safety Act' among her public-safety-related record. However, no source in the available material describes this bill's substance as specifically making fleeing from law enforcement a federal crime; that description appears to be an added detail not substantiated by the record. Since the underlying fact that she supported this named officer-safety-related legislation is confirmed, this is a narrow, minor inaccuracy in describing the bill's specific content rather than a fabrication of her overall record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks was Iowa Department of Public Health Director from 2010 to 2014
description: She served as Iowa Department of Public Health Director from 2010 to 2013, not 2010 to 2014, resigning to run for Congress.

inaccurate_statement: Served 24 years in the U.S. Army as a private, nurse, and physician.
description: Miller-Meeks served in the U.S. Army from 1974 to 1982 (Army Medical Department, retiring as a Lieutenant Colonel) and then in the Army Reserve from 1983 to 2000. While a combined 24-year figure roughly matches her total active and reserve service, describing her as having served solely 'as a private, nurse, and physician' omits and mischaracterizes her actual career path, which included retiring as a Lieutenant Colonel and holding significant rank, not remaining a private. This is a narrow mischaracterization of her military career progression rather than a wholesale fabrication.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks won in 2024 by an extremely narrow margin—50.0% to 49.8% over Bohannan
description: Miller-Meeks won the 2024 race by 799 votes (about 0.2%) after a recount, which is consistent with an extremely close race, but the specific percentages cited (50.0% to 49.8%) are not confirmed against the source material, which describes the margin only in vote count/percentage terms of roughly 0.2%. The overall characterization of a razor-thin 2024 win is accurate, but the precise percentage figures are unverified and could be imprecise.

The response also omits Bridgford's standing in the poll entirely, misrepresenting it as a simple two-way result.

inaccurate_statement: A July 16 Bullfinch Group/Independent Center poll had Bohannan ahead 45%–40%

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan is clearly to the left of Miller-Meeks on abortion, Medicaid/ACA policy, and immigration, even if her overall presentation is moderate
description: On abortion and Medicaid/ACA policy, this is well supported by the record (Bohannan supports codifying Roe-era protections and reversing Medicaid cuts, while Miller-Meeks co-sponsored the Life at Conception Act and voted for the OBBBA's Medicaid provisions). However, on immigration specifically, the characterization is less clear-cut: both candidates support border security paired with some reform, and Bohannan has explicitly said border security is important and criticized Biden as too slow on the border, while also supporting a pathway to citizenship — a nuanced position that isn't simply 'to the left' of Miller-Meeks's own support for some Dreamer protections. This blanket claim oversimplifies a more mixed comparative picture on immigration specifically, though it doesn't fundamentally mischaracterize either candidate's broader positioning.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has increasingly aligned herself with Trump and the current Republican agenda, which makes her less moderate on some national issues than her earlier profile
description: While Miller-Meeks received Trump's full endorsement and has voted with her party on major bills like the 2025 reconciliation bill, characterizing her as having become markedly less moderate is contestable given her documented record: she chairs the Conservative Climate Caucus, belongs to the moderate Republican Governance Group, has a mixed/tension-filled record on clean-energy tax credits (she lobbied to preserve them before voting for a bill rolling many back), and has a real bipartisan legislative record (EARLY Act Reauthorization, Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act with a Democrat, opioid-prevention bill with Democrats). This is a subjective characterization presented with some confidence rather than a clean, verifiable fact, and cuts against the documented internal tensions in her record rather than a simple rightward drift.

inaccurate_statement: Christina Bohannan is a moderate Democrat by Iowa standards, particularly compared with the national Democratic left, and is closer to the center of the Democratic caucus than many national Democrats
description: Available research characterizes Bohannan as progressive/liberal rather than moderate. A political ideology tracker labels her a 'Progressive Democrat,' her record shows 'a consistent tilt toward progressive policy goals,' and even her own pushback is that she isn't 'radical' rather than that she is moderate. While she has more recently worked to present herself as pragmatic and reach rural/conservative voters, this is described as a deliberate campaign strategy and messaging shift rather than an already-settled characterization of her as a moderate within the Democratic caucus.

inaccurate_statement: Mariannette Miller-Meeks is generally viewed as the most conventionally moderate/centrist of the two major-party candidates, particularly on fiscal and social-policy issues
description: This characterization is contested and not well supported, especially regarding social policy. Miller-Meeks co-sponsored the federal Life at Conception Act, an extreme, no-exceptions abortion ban framing used by critics, and while she belongs to some relatively moderate House GOP caucuses suggesting some fiscal centrism, her 'moderate' branding is itself described in reporting as contested political messaging rather than settled fact. She is frequently branded 'extreme' by opponents on abortion specifically, undercutting a blanket claim that she is the more moderate candidate overall.

inaccurate_statement: Christina Bohannan's positions on abortion rights, Medicaid expansion, and other Democratic priorities place her to the left of Miller-Meeks on several major issues, making her a mainstream Democrat with more clearly progressive positions
description: Bohannan has deliberately worked to counter a 'radical progressive' label by emphasizing moderate economic messaging, acknowledging that Republicans 'sometimes have a point' on regulation and spending, and campaigning heavily on affordability and bipartisan themes; reporting frames her as pushing back against being cast to the left rather than simply confirming that framing. Describing her without any of this context as simply having 'more clearly progressive positions' one-sidedly resolves a contested characterization.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is generally viewed as a moderate Republican relative to many GOP members, with a focus on bipartisan healthcare issues contributing to that image
description: This characterization is disputed rather than settled fact. Miller-Meeks co-sponsored the federal Life at Conception Act and supported Iowa's restrictive abortion law, which critics and reporting specifically cite as evidence that her 'moderate' branding does not hold up on social policy, even though she does belong to relatively centrist House GOP caucuses on some fiscal matters. Presenting her as clearly and generally 'moderate' without acknowledging this contested record overstates a one-sided framing as settled fact.

inaccurate_statement: A May poll had Bohannan ahead 32%-28.3% over Miller-Meeks, with a sizable undecided bloc
description: No evidence supports a May poll showing Bohannan at 32% and Miller-Meeks at 28.3%. The only verified three-way poll with these candidates is the Bullfinch Group survey from mid-July 2026, showing different, rounder figures (Bohannan 40%, Miller-Meeks 35%, Bridgford 11%). No May poll with this specific breakdown could be found by any tracked source, and this figure appears to be fabricated.

inaccurate_statement: A current forecast (Independent Center Voice) gives Bohannan roughly a 70-75% modeled chance of winning
description: No forecasting model or organization called 'Independent Center Voice' (or similarly named entity) issuing a 70-75% modeled win probability for Bohannan could be verified. The real organization 'Independent Center Voice' publishes district polling but does not issue candidate win-probability forecasts; nonpartisan forecasters (Cook Political Report, Sabato's Crystal Ball, Inside Elections) all rate the race as a toss-up rather than assigning Bohannan a specific 70-75% chance.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks' state elected experience is described simply as 'Iowa state senator (2019–2020)'
description: Miller-Meeks was elected to the Iowa Senate in 2018 and served in Iowa Senate District 41 from January 2019 until January 2021, when she resigned to take her U.S. House seat; describing her term end as 2020 rather than early 2021 is a minor date imprecision but not a significant misrepresentation.

inaccurate_statement: Davenport had 565 violent crimes per 100,000 residents in 2023 data cited in the response
description: Available sourcing places Davenport's violent-crime rate around 581 per 100,000 (2024 reporting), not the 565 figure cited here for 2023; this is a narrow statistical discrepancy about a district-wide crime statistic rather than a claim about either candidate's record.

description: No evidence supports Miller-Meeks backing mandatory E-Verify as part of her immigration platform. Her official House Border Security page details an extensive list of her immigration votes and cosponsorships (SAVE Act, Laken Riley Act, Secure the Border Act, HALT Fentanyl Act, Mayorkas impeachment, etc.) but makes no mention of E-Verify, and she is not a cosponsor of the primary federal E-Verify mandate bill. This is a narrow addition to an otherwise accurate general characterization of her as an immigration hawk, so it doesn't change the overall picture of her stated positions.

inaccurate_statement: One 2026 analysis found 42% of non-party-affiliated voters in IA-01 identifying immigration as a priority, per Independent Center Voice
description: The actual Independent Center Voice/Bullfinch Group survey of IA-01 voters found immigration was cited as a top issue by only about 10-15% of voters (including independents), not 42%. No source contains a 42% figure for non-party-affiliated voters and immigration in this district; this specific statistic does not match the real survey data and appears to be a fabricated or garbled figure, though it does not change the broader accurate point that immigration is a genuine issue in the race.

This is a narrow point about a third-party figure rather than about either main candidate's own record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is a 24-year Army veteran
description: This is duplicated in the accurate list because it is directly confirmed by the dossier ('U.S. Army 1974–1982... then Army Reserve 1983–2000'), which totals roughly 26 years of combined active/reserve service, close to but not exactly matching '24-year.' This is a minor rounding discrepancy, not a substantive error.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks secured NDAA provisions concerning artillery production
description: The record confirms Miller-Meeks secured amendments in the FY2027 NDAA related to Iowa's defense infrastructure, military readiness, and the Rock Island Arsenal, but no source specifically documents an 'artillery production' provision as distinct from the general Rock Island Arsenal/defense workforce funding already confirmed. This appears to be an embellished detail not independently verifiable.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is a member of the Ukraine Caucus
description: The record documents Miller-Meeks as chair of the Conservative Climate Caucus, co-chair of the Pandemic Preparedness Caucus, and a member of the Republican Governance Group, Climate Solutions Caucus, Pro-Life Caucus, and Taiwan Caucus. No 'Ukraine Caucus' membership is documented for her.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks explicitly supported Taiwan's security and reducing U.S. dependence on China
description: While Miller-Meeks's Taiwan Caucus membership and general hawkish-on-China orientation are documented, no specific direct statement about 'reducing U.S. dependence on China' as a distinct national-security position (as opposed to her documented manufacturing/supply-chain statements) is confirmed in the record; this presents an inferred position with some hedging as more concrete than documented.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has argued for alliances and international engagement, including support for partners such as Ukraine, but less of her public campaign platform is centered on military readiness/defense policy, implying this reflects her own stated position rather than inference from party alignment
description: Bohannan has made some documented statements supporting Ukraine and international alliances, but a comprehensive, itemized position on broader national-security topics like military readiness, China/Taiwan, or NATO alliances is not established as a defined platform plank in her available record; presenting her general foreign-policy leanings as a settled comparative position risks overstating what is actually a thin public record on this topic, distinct from a fabrication but bordering on an unhedged inference.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supported the 2027 NDAA, including measures involving Iowa's defense infrastructure
description: Miller-Meeks's documented support and secured amendments relate to the FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act (voted on/passed in 2026 for fiscal year 2027), and coverage refers to it as the FY2027 NDAA rather than "the 2027 NDAA" in a way that could be misread as a bill enacted in the year 2027. This is a minor terminology imprecision rather than a substantive misrepresentation of her record, since she did support the relevant defense authorization legislation and secured Iowa-specific defense provisions.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supports tariffs as part of a broader protectionist/manufacturing strategy.
description: Miller-Meeks's actual voting record on tariffs is more adversarial to blanket tariff support than this framing suggests: she voted three times to block House consideration of ending Trump's tariff emergency declarations and voted against ending the Canada tariff emergency specifically, but she has also blamed the 2024-2025 Quad Cities manufacturing layoffs (e.g., John Deere) on "a lack of robust trade policy" and high interest rates rather than embracing tariffs as her chosen strategy, and her own fertilizer-tariff-cutting bill (the "Lowering Input Costs for American Farmers Act") cuts against a simple 'pro-tariff protectionist' characterization. This is a mischaracterization of a genuinely more mixed and internally tense record, not a wholesale fabrication, so it is minor rather than critical.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks argues that the 2025 tax legislation is benefiting Iowa manufacturing workers and has received support from manufacturing-oriented business groups.
description: While Miller-Meeks did support the 2025 tax legislation (OBBBA) and has touted small-business tax provisions, and did receive an August 2026 U.S. Chamber of Commerce endorsement citing her work for Iowa businesses, the specific framing that manufacturing-oriented business groups have endorsed her because of the tax law's benefit to manufacturing workers is an inference beyond what is documented; her office's specific district figures on the tax law's business benefits are about small/pass-through businesses generally rather than manufacturing workers specifically, and the U.S. Chamber endorsement cites broader pro-growth tax policy and small-business engagement, not manufacturing-specific praise.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan opposed Iowa legislation providing qualified immunity to police
description: Bohannan's opposition to the 2021 'Back the Blue' law (SF 342) was not centered on opposing a grant of qualified immunity to police as the response implies. Her documented rationale focused on concerns that the bill would undermine public trust, pit police against protesters, and potentially make communities less safe or infringe civil liberties -- not a specific objection framed around qualified immunity itself. Characterizing her vote as being about 'opposing qualified immunity for police' mischaracterizes the actual substance and stated rationale of her position on this bill.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks voted four times for federal legislation that included a 10-year restriction on state/local AI regulation, which critics argue could have limited Iowa and local governments' ability to impose additional data-center requirements.
description: The dossier for Miller-Meeks documents no such specific voting record of 'four times' voting for a 10-year federal moratorium on state/local AI regulation. It does note she voted against amendments that would have preserved a state/local AI data-center moratorium in committee proceedings (per an advocacy group's account) and that she has faced criticism for votes seen as blocking local data-center restrictions, but the specific claim of a '10-year restriction' voted on 'four times' is not substantiated by the available record and appears to be an invented level of specificity not found in the source material.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan favors investing heavily in advanced law enforcement tools, such as high-energy scanners, to detect fentanyl hidden inside commercial trucks and passenger vehicles at ports of entry, and has said fentanyl is trafficked mostly through legal ports of entry
description: While Bohannan has generally supported more Border Patrol agents and fentanyl-interdiction equipment and greater processing capacity at ports of entry, the specific framing in the response attributing to her a detailed claim about 'high-energy scanners' for detecting fentanyl in commercial trucks goes beyond what is confirmed as her own direct statement; this level of specificity was not verified against a primary source in the underlying research.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has specifically called for expanding border inspection equipment to detect fentanyl and increasing Border Patrol resources
description: Miller-Meeks's documented positions on fentanyl and border security center on cosponsoring and voting for the HALT Fentanyl Act, supporting the Laken Riley Act, the Secure the Border Act, finishing border wall construction, and general enforcement messaging. There is no confirmed record of her specifically calling for 'expanding border inspection equipment to detect fentanyl' as a distinct, named proposal; this appears to be an unverified or invented specific detail layered onto her broader, real enforcement-focused record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has supported requiring employers to use E-Verify
description: No evidence supports this claim. Miller-Meeks's own official House 'Border Security' issues page details her immigration votes and positions (SAVE Act, Laken Riley Act, Secure the Border Act, HALT Fentanyl Act, Mayorkas impeachment, etc.) but makes no mention of E-Verify. Searches for Miller-Meeks combined with E-Verify turn up no press releases, votes, or statements linking her to mandatory E-Verify advocacy, and she is not a cosponsor of the primary federal E-Verify mandate bill. This is a narrow addition that doesn't change the overall accurate picture that she is an immigration-enforcement hawk.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan proposes adding home-health benefits to Medicare
description: Bohannan's documented Medicare expansion proposal is to add dental, hearing, and vision coverage to Medicare, not home-health benefits. No source ties her platform to a home-health Medicare expansion; this appears to be an inaccurate addition to an otherwise correctly described set of proposals.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks is a former nurse
description: Mariannette Miller-Meeks holds a nursing degree (BSN from Texas Christian University) but her documented professional and political career is as a physician (ophthalmologist) — she ran a private ophthalmology practice in Ottumwa, Iowa, and is described in her biography as a physician, not as someone who practiced as a nurse. Describing her as a 'former nurse' in addition to physician is not supported by her documented career history.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has proposed expanding Medicare coverage to include home-health benefits
description: Bohannan's documented Medicare expansion proposal adds dental, hearing, and vision coverage alongside a Medicare buy-in at any age. No source ties her to a home-health-benefits expansion specifically; this appears to substitute an incorrect benefit category for her actual, well-documented position.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan proposes adding home-health benefits to Medicare (bundled with dental, vision, hearing)
description: Bohannan's well-documented Medicare expansion proposal is to add dental, hearing, and vision coverage alongside a Medicare buy-in at any age. No source ties her to a specific proposal to add home-health benefits to Medicare; this appears to be an inaccurate addition to an otherwise correctly described platform item.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's broader platform calls for substantial public investment in infrastructure, particularly school infrastructure, and emphasizes jobs, manufacturing and organized labor, implying this is her stated roads/highways position.
description: Bohannan's campaign platform contains no direct statement on roads, bridges, or highway infrastructure as a standalone 2026 policy position — this is a confirmed, documented gap after repeated dedicated searches of her full campaign site. Her platform does emphasize public school investment, but framing 'school infrastructure' investment as effectively her roads/highways stance conflates two unrelated policy areas and presents an inference as if it were her substantiated position.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks secured $1 million for the U.S. Highway 6/Deer Creek Road intersection
description: Reporting on this Community Project Funding request indicates $1 million was secured toward a larger $4.9 million request for this intersection project; this figure itself is consistent with the dossier, so no correction needed beyond noting the request context is omitted, which is a peripheral detail.

inaccurate_statement: Her campaign says her opposition to Iowa's 2021 'Back the Blue' law was because she believed it could jeopardize local police funding and safety
description: Bohannan's actual stated objections to the 2021 Back the Blue bill centered on protecting the right to protest, concerns about pitting law enforcement against racial-justice demonstrators, and fears the bill could undermine public trust and civil liberties -- not a stated concern about jeopardizing local police funding specifically. This mischaracterizes the substance of her rationale, though it does not reverse the basic fact that she voted against the bill.

inaccurate_statement: She also voted against the 2021 legislation providing qualified immunity for police
description: Bohannan's documented 2021 vote was against Iowa's 'Back the Blue' bill (SF 342), which included qualified-immunity-related provisions among a broader package addressing law enforcement, protest penalties, and other issues -- it was not itself a standalone 'qualified immunity' bill, and describing it as separate legislation "providing qualified immunity" she voted against, distinct from the previously mentioned Back the Blue vote, creates a misleading impression of two separate votes when there was one.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks secured federal funding for local public-safety projects, including a $499,873 DOJ Byrne grant for the Oskaloosa Safe City Project
description: The funding Miller-Meeks secured for Oskaloosa's SAFECity Initiative is documented across multiple sources as $500,000, described as a Community Project Funding appropriation she secured, not as a $499,873 DOJ Byrne grant. No source ties this project to a specific $499,873 figure or characterizes it as a Byrne Justice Assistance Grant; the well-documented figure and mechanism differ from what is claimed here.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks' official 'Economy' platform page contains an explicit unemployment-reduction plan comparable in specificity to Bohannan's workforce-development plan
description: Miller-Meeks's official economy platform emphasizes energy production, manufacturing tax policy, and small-business tax cuts, but contains no explicit statement addressing the unemployment rate as such—this is a documented gap, not a fully developed unemployment plan. The response's framing implying she has a clear, quantified unemployment strategy overstates what exists, though it does correctly note her general pro-business, tax-cut theory of job creation.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks previously opposed legislation requiring expanded monitoring for PFAS
description: No record exists of Miller-Meeks taking a specific position on PFAS monitoring legislation. Her documented record shows no direct 2026 statement on Iowa's nitrate/water crisis specifically, and her water-related positions found are about wetlands/waterway regulation (WOTUS) and general infrastructure funding, not a specific vote or statement opposing PFAS monitoring requirements. This appears to be an unsupported claim rather than a verified part of her record.

inaccurate_statement: A district analysis specifically identifies tariffs and rising prices as challenges for IA-01 manufacturers employing more than 65,000 workers
description: No source in the available research corroborates a specific figure of '65,000 workers' employed by IA-01 manufacturers, nor an analysis framing tariffs and rising prices as a challenge tied to that specific employment figure. While manufacturing job losses (e.g., Whirlpool layoffs) are a well-documented and real issue in the race, this specific statistic could not be verified and appears to be an unsupported or fabricated figure.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's economic approach is more focused on limiting federal spending and regulation, and she voted against funding new infrastructure projects
description: Miller-Meeks's opposition to the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law was specifically about its cost and bundling with non-transportation spending, not a blanket opposition to infrastructure funding. In fact, she has a substantial documented record of securing and touting infrastructure/community project funding for IA-01 (over $87.1 million since taking office, including specific road, bridge, and wastewater projects). Describing her as having simply 'voted against funding new infrastructure projects' omits this significant countervailing record and mischaracterizes a nuanced position as a blanket anti-infrastructure stance.

inaccurate_statement: A district analysis specifically identifies tariffs and rising prices as challenges for IA-01 manufacturers employing more than 65,000 workers
description: No source in the available research corroborates a specific figure of '65,000 workers' employed by IA-01 manufacturers, nor an analysis framing tariffs and rising prices as a challenge tied to that specific employment figure. While manufacturing job losses (e.g., Whirlpool layoffs) are a well-documented and real issue in the race, this specific statistic could not be verified and appears to be an unsupported or fabricated figure.

inaccurate_statement: the available candidate comparisons emphasize her healthcare and economic-policy record rather than a specific new "local jobs" plan
description: Mariannette Miller-Meeks has a documented, confirmed record of statements specifically addressing local manufacturing jobs, including direct comments on the John Deere/Quad Cities layoffs attributing them to trade and economic policy factors, praise for Vermeer's Iowa expansion, a completed 'Made in America Manufacturing Tour,' the Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act, and securing funding for the Lee County Career Center workforce-training facility. Portraying her as lacking a jobs-specific platform and only having a general healthcare/economic record omits this documented, direct record on local jobs and manufacturing.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's platform emphasizes domestic manufacturing, reducing regulations, expanding domestic energy, and policies she says will keep manufacturing jobs in the U.S., with the clearest domestic-manufacturing/job-retention agenda in the race
description: Miller-Meeks does have documented positions on domestic manufacturing (the Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act, ONSHORE Act, energy production emphasis) and has commented on Quad Cities layoffs, but her official economy platform has no explicit statement on the unemployment rate as such, and there is a documented internal tension where she blames trade/tariff policy for job losses while repeatedly voting to preserve the very tariff emergency declarations criticized for raising costs on manufacturers. Presenting her as having unambiguously 'the clearest' and 'most direct' job-retention platform, without any of this nuance, overstates the strength and clarity of her record relative to what is actually documented.

inaccurate_statement: One 2026 IA-01 voter analysis found 42% of NPP (no-party-preference) voters citing immigration as a priority
description: The only identifiable 2026 IA-01-specific survey with issue-priority crosstabs by party affiliation (the Independent Center Voice/Independent Leadership Council poll conducted by the Bullfinch Group in July 2026) shows that independent voters ranked immigration as their most pressing issue at only about 10-15%, not 42%, and the survey does not use 'NPP' terminology. No source corroborates a 42% figure for immigration as a priority among non-party-affiliated IA-01 voters; this specific statistic appears to be fabricated or a data error repeated across multiple research passes on this race.

inaccurate_statement: One 2026 IA-01 voter analysis found 42% of NPP (no-party-preference) voters citing immigration as a priority
description: The only identifiable 2026 IA-01-specific survey with issue-priority crosstabs by party affiliation (the Independent Center Voice/Independent Leadership Council poll conducted by the Bullfinch Group in July 2026) shows that independent voters ranked immigration as their most pressing issue at only about 10-15%, not 42%, and the survey does not use 'NPP' terminology. No source corroborates a 42% figure for immigration as a priority among non-party-affiliated IA-01 voters; this specific statistic appears to be fabricated or a data error repeated across multiple research passes on this race.

inaccurate_statement: One district-level analysis reports 42% of NPP/independent voters naming immigration as a priority
description: The actual Independent Center Voice IA-01 survey found immigration was cited as the top pressing issue by only about 10-15% of independent/non-party voters (figures vary slightly by version of the analysis found), not 42%. No survey or analysis has been found supporting a 42% figure for this subgroup on this issue; this specific statistic appears to be a recurring fabricated or erroneous statistic not grounded in the actual polling data.

inaccurate_statement: A May district survey found affordability among the issues independents are focused on, with 77.9% of respondents saying a candidate's positions matter at least as much as party affiliation, and 66.2% saying they were open to an independent candidate who would work with both parties

No survey or analysis has been found supporting a 42% figure for this subgroup on this issue; this specific statistic appears to be a recurring fabricated or erroneous statistic not grounded in the actual polling data.
