inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks led legislation providing Medicare coverage for multi-cancer early-detection (MCED) tests
description: The Nancy Gardner Sewell Medicare Multi-Cancer Early Detection Screening Coverage Act was introduced by Rep. Jodey Arrington (R-TX), with Miller-Meeks as one of several original cosponsors, not the lead sponsor. However, her own congressional press releases and some local news outlets do describe her as having 'led' or championed the bill, so this is a contested framing rather than a clear fabrication, and the bill's substance and her substantive role are accurately described elsewhere in the response.

inaccurate_statement: Mariannette Miller-Meeks has sponsored legislation placing limits on chokeholds
description: As an Iowa state senator, Miller-Meeks supported bipartisan state legislation that banned chokeholds and increased implicit-bias training. However, there is no record of her sponsoring federal legislation on chokeholds during her time in Congress, and no confirmed source ties a specific chokehold-limiting bill to her congressional record. This overstates a real but narrower state-level record as a broader legislative sponsorship claim.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supports E-Verify as part of her border/immigration platform
description: No evidence supports that Miller-Meeks has backed mandatory E-Verify as part of her border/immigration platform. Her official House Border Security issues page details her votes and cosponsorships (SAVE Act, Laken Riley Act, Secure the Border Act, HALT Fentanyl Act, Mayorkas impeachment) but makes no mention of E-Verify, and no press releases or statements tie her to this specific policy.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks supports using E-Verify
description: No evidence in Miller-Meeks's documented record supports mandatory E-Verify as part of her platform. Her official House border-security page and legislative record cover the wall, catch-and-release, asylum limits, and ICE/DHS funding, but no source ties her to E-Verify advocacy specifically; this appears to be an added detail not attributable to her actual platform.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's platform is characterized as having no itemized small-business plan comparable to Miller-Meeks, implicitly framing her jobs agenda as broader but less targeted, without noting she also has confirmed direct statements on manufacturing jobs (John Deere/Quad Cities) and vocational training
description: Bohannan has a confirmed, direct statement specifically addressing manufacturing job losses in the Quad Cities (John Deere layoffs) and pledges to expand vocational/technical training to grow high-skill, high-wage jobs — a more targeted jobs-related position than the response's framing (which characterizes her approach as general wage/cost improvement rather than direct job creation) fully credits.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's official economy platform has no explicit itemized unemployment-rate-focused statement, but the response presents her platform as 'more explicitly centered on' job creation/lowering unemployment without noting this gap
description: Miller-Meeks's official House 'Economy' issues page emphasizes energy production, manufacturing tax policy, and small-business tax cuts, but contains no explicit statement addressing the unemployment rate as such — a documented gap. Presenting her plan as clearly and directly aimed at lowering unemployment overstates the specificity of her actual platform, though the broader thrust (pro-growth, tax/regulatory-focused economic policy) is accurately characterized.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's approach is centered on tax incentives and other pro-business policies intended to encourage companies to expand and hire, plus expanding domestic manufacturing and keeping production in the U.S., framed as her general economy/jobs plan
description: Miller-Meeks's official economy platform emphasizes energy production, the Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act, small-business tax cuts, and housing affordability, but her official page contains no explicit statement addressing the unemployment rate as such -- this is a documented gap. The response presents a specific unemployment-reduction mechanism as her stated plan without noting this gap or hedging that it is inferred from her general tax/business/manufacturing positions.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks's jobs approach includes infrastructure and development spending, which she argues supports construction, transportation, agriculture and local businesses, as part of a plan to reduce unemployment
description: There is no confirmed direct statement from Miller-Meeks framing infrastructure/development spending explicitly as an unemployment-reduction mechanism; her documented infrastructure record is presented as a delivery track record (specific funded local projects) rather than a forward-looking jobs/unemployment plan, and this framing overstates the connection without hedging.

inaccurate_statement: The American Cancer Society's Iowa advocacy arm says that raising the tobacco tax is the single most impactful public-health policy it sees for reducing cancer and deaths
description: This specific 'single most impactful public health intervention' framing was said by Dr. Mary Charlton, a University of Iowa epidemiology professor and director of the Iowa Cancer Registry, during a March 2026 legislative committee meeting — not by the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network (ACS CAN), the ACS's Iowa advocacy arm. ACS CAN does advocate for tobacco tax increases as an effective tobacco-control measure, but the specific superlative claim attributed here belongs to a different person/organization.

inaccurate_statement: The American Cancer Society's Iowa advocacy arm says that raising the tobacco tax is the single most impactful public-health policy it sees for reducing cancer and deaths
description: This specific 'single most impactful public health intervention' framing was said by Dr. Mary Charlton, a University of Iowa epidemiology professor and director of the Iowa Cancer Registry, during a March 2026 legislative committee meeting — not by the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network (ACS CAN), the ACS's Iowa advocacy arm. ACS CAN does advocate for tobacco tax increases as an effective tobacco-control measure, but the specific superlative claim attributed here belongs to a different person/organization.

inaccurate_statement: A 2026 voter guide characterizes Bohannan as favoring tighter environmental regulation, while Miller-Meeks has supported loosening some environmental protections
description: While it is true Miller-Meeks has opposed WOTUS/Clean Water Act expansion and Bohannan has an explicit PFAS/nitrate reduction plank, describing Bohannan as favoring mandatory 'tighter environmental regulation' overstates her documented position — she has explicitly said she prefers working with farmers through incentives and funded conservation practices rather than imposing mandates, criticizing a tendency to 'regulate first and ask questions later.' This nuance is missing from the binary regulation-versus-deregulation framing presented.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks says her total Community Project Funding in the district includes substantial investments in modernizing water systems
description: Miller-Meeks's documented water-related project funding is narrower than 'substantial investments in modernizing water systems' suggests — it consists of specific, itemized items such as $3 million for the Davenport Water Pollution Control Plant and $2 million for a Muscatine wastewater force main, which are flood-mitigation/wastewater infrastructure projects, not a broad or substantial modernization program. There is no dedicated 2026 statement from her addressing the nitrate/agricultural-runoff crisis specifically, which the response otherwise correctly notes is a gap.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has supported E-Verify as part of her immigration platform
description: There is no evidence Miller-Meeks has backed mandatory E-Verify. Her own official House Border Security issues page, which extensively details her immigration votes and cosponsorships, makes no mention of E-Verify, and she is not a cosponsor of the primary federal E-Verify mandate bill. This appears to be an unsupported addition to an otherwise accurate description of her enforcement-focused record.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's approach 'has generally put more emphasis on constitutional limits, accountability, and avoiding policies that unnecessarily pit protesters against police,' implying her record is 'therefore less aligned with a traditional "more policing + tougher enforcement" definition of public safety'
description: This framing selectively emphasizes Bohannan's 2021 opposition to the 'Back the Blue' bill while omitting that she also supports funding local law enforcement with adequate training and resources, introduced legislation supporting officers injured on the job, and voted for tougher penalties for drug dealers and human traffickers. Presenting her record as generally less supportive of traditional policing understates these documented pro-police-funding elements of her record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks secured more than $3 million specifically for the Oskaloosa SAFECity Initiative
description: The Oskaloosa SAFECity Initiative funding Miller-Meeks secured is documented at $500,000, not more than $3 million. The $500,000 figure covers license-plate readers, body and in-car cameras, police-facility upgrades, school panic buttons, real-time crime monitoring, and a search-and-rescue drone. No source ties a $3 million figure to this specific Oskaloosa project; this appears to be an inflated or conflated dollar amount.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks voted for measures to build 900 miles of border wall
description: Miller-Meeks's documented border-security record includes support for finishing border wall construction and voting for the Secure the Border Act, but no source ties her to a specific '900 miles' figure for wall construction she voted to build. This specific numeric detail does not appear in her documented record.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks voted for measures requiring E-Verify for new hires
description: Research into Miller-Meeks's border/immigration record found no evidence she has backed or voted for mandatory E-Verify legislation. Her documented record centers on the Laken Riley Act, Secure the Border Act, SAVE Act, HALT Fentanyl Act, and wall-completion legislation, none of which involve E-Verify mandates.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has backed mandatory E-Verify for employers hiring new workers
description: No evidence supports this claim. Miller-Meeks's own official House 'Border Security' issues page provides an extensive, detailed list of her immigration/border votes and cosponsorships but makes no mention of E-Verify at all, and she is not a cosponsor of the primary federal bill mandating nationwide E-Verify. This is a narrow addition to an otherwise accurate general characterization of her as an immigration hawk.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has made the Farm Bill and family-farm succession a prominent part of her current agriculture agenda.
description: Miller-Meeks's documented agriculture record centers on fertilizer-tariff relief, E15/ethanol advocacy, and voting for the 2026 farm bill (Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026), with tax-policy provisions (estate tax/stepped-up basis protections) supporting family-farm succession as a genuine but secondary element via broader tax legislation. Casting 'family-farm succession' as a 'prominent' standalone piece of her current agriculture agenda overstates its centrality relative to her better-documented fertilizer-cost and trade-focused efforts.

inaccurate_statement: Farm Action Fund endorsed Bohannan in July and specifically cited her position on monopoly power in seed, fertilizer and meatpacking
description: A farm-advocacy group's Rural Independence Initiative (part of Farm Action Fund) is documented as endorsing Bohannan, but no source confirms the endorsement announcement specifically cited her position on monopoly power in seed, fertilizer, and meatpacking as the stated rationale; this specific framing of the endorsement's justification is unverified and not established in the available record.

inaccurate_statement: Iowa could potentially receive about $1 billion over five years from the Rural Health Transformation Program
description: The dossier documents an initial $209 million Iowa allocation from the $50 billion federal Rural Health Transformation Program, but does not confirm a specific five-year total of approximately $1 billion for Iowa. This projected total figure is not substantiated in the available material and appears to be an unverified extrapolation.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has a prior Iowa legislative record that she describes as supporting small businesses
description: Research found no itemized small-business plan or specific legislative record on small-business support attributable to Bohannan; her campaign site references being a general champion for small businesses within broader affordability/farm-economy planks, but no specific itemized small-business policy or legislative record framing exists. This is a genuine, confirmed gap rather than a documented record she 'describes' as supporting small businesses.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan's background makes her more aligned with calls for stronger oversight of large data centers, including concerns about water use, electricity demand, tax incentives, and local control, implying this is effectively her stance on data center development
description: Bohannan has no documented public statement, vote, or campaign position on data center development despite dedicated research into her campaign site, social media, and news coverage of the live Clinton, Iowa data-center controversy within her district. Presenting an inference from her environmental engineering background as effectively her actual stance on this issue is speculative rather than a verified position.

inaccurate_statement: Her primary challenger, David Pautsch, accused her of being dishonest about her residence, and Iowa law permits people with multiple residences some flexibility regarding voter registration
description: The documented residency controversy centered on a Bettendorf resident who filed a residency challenge with the Scott County board and an Office of Congressional Ethics complaint in fall 2024, not primarily on accusations from primary challenger David Pautsch. The response attributes the core allegation to the wrong source, though Pautsch has separately criticized her in other contexts. The core underlying facts about the residency inconsistency (Ottumwa homestead credit while registering elsewhere, later re-registering outside IA-01) are real, but this specific attribution of who raised the residency dishonesty allegation is not supported.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks drew criticism from some Republicans, including primary challenger David Pautsch, for certifying the 2020 election results and supporting an independent commission to investigate the January 6 attack.
description: No record exists of Miller-Meeks facing criticism from David Pautsch or other Republicans specifically over certifying the 2020 election results or supporting a January 6 independent commission. Her documented controversies include a residency/voter-registration inconsistency, a town-hall accessibility controversy, self-corrected "no tax on Social Security" messaging, and a 2021 financial-disclosure ethics complaint from the Iowa Democratic Party. Her 2026 primary opponent Pautsch's documented dispute with her involved an FEC complaint over a misleading mass text message, not election-certification or January 6 commission criticism. This appears to be a fabricated detail not supported by available research.

inaccurate_statement: I found less recent evidence of a comparable schedule of open, traditional town-hall-style events [for Miller-Meeks]
description: Miller-Meeks's accessibility record is more specifically documented than the response suggests: she avoided in-person town halls for most of 2025 (reportedly saying she'd hold one 'when hell freezes over'), then held one contentious in-person town hall in Keosauqua on November 10, 2025, while also conducting substantial tele-town halls reaching thousands of participants at a time. The response's vague framing of 'less recent evidence' undersells the extent to which her avoidance of open town halls is a well-documented, specific controversy rather than simply an information gap.

inaccurate_statement: There is less evidence of the kind of accessible, open town-hall-style engagement from Miller-Meeks, implying she holds no town halls or comparable accessibility events
description: Miller-Meeks has held tele-town halls reaching thousands of participants (one reported at 10,700, others at 6,300, 8,000, and 13,000) and completed a 20-county in-person tour, plus one contentious in-person town hall in Keosauqua in November 2025. She avoided in-person town halls for most of 2025 and used a moderator-filtered format that critics said screened out hard questions, which is a legitimate basis for criticism, but the response's framing implies she has essentially no accessibility events at all, which understates her substantial tele-town-hall record and omits the one in-person town hall she did hold.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has 'strongest documented history of formal constituent access (town halls...)' and 'has held public...constituent events' emphasizing accessibility, implying a robust, uncontroversial town hall record
description: This claim inverts the well-documented record. Miller-Meeks avoided in-person town halls for most of 2025, telling a local GOP meeting she'd hold one 'when hell freezes over.' Her first in-person town hall of that period, held in November 2025 in Keosauqua, was widely reported as contentious, with booing, heckling, and an attendee removed, and used a written-question/moderator-filtered format critics said screened out hard questions. She relies primarily on tele-town halls rather than open in-person forums. Presenting her as having the clearly 'strongest' and most accessible town hall record, without any of this context, is a significant mischaracterization that would mislead a reader about her actual accessibility record.

inaccurate_statement: Christina Bohannan takes corporate PAC money, just less than Miller-Meeks, citing her ~$491,928 in PAC/other committee receipts as evidence
description: Bohannan's total PAC/other-committee receipts of about $491,928 is accurate as a raw dollar figure, but presenting this as evidence she takes 'corporate PAC money' is misleading. A detailed review of her itemized FEC Schedule A contributions shows every identified PAC/committee contributor traces to Democratic joint-fundraising or ideological vehicles (such as House Victory Project 2026 and 314 Action Impact Slate), not corporate or trade-association PACs. Her stated pledge to take no corporate PAC money holds up against her primary-source filings, so characterizing her PAC receipts as partial evidence of accepting corporate PAC money mischaracterizes the nature of that funding.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks' campaign reported $83,700 from corporate PACs in the second half of 2025
description: No source supports this specific $83,700 figure for corporate PAC money to Miller-Meeks during any 2025 reporting period. Documented figures for that period differ substantially (e.g., $107,500 in corporate PAC money in Q1 2025 alone, per Iowa Starting Line). The broader point that she accepts corporate PAC money is accurate, but this specific number appears to be fabricated or erroneous.

inaccurate_statement: David Pautsch (Republican challenger) and Travis Terrell (Democrat) are presented as current candidates in the IA-01 race with active endorsement lists.
description: Both David Pautsch and Travis Terrell were defeated in their respective party primaries in June 2026 (Pautsch lost to Miller-Meeks by more than 40 points; Terrell lost to Bohannan by roughly 81-82%) and are not on the November 2026 general election ballot. The actual 2026 IA-01 general election field consists of Miller-Meeks (R), Bohannan (D), and independent Michael Bridgford. Presenting Pautsch and Terrell as current candidates with ongoing endorsement activity misrepresents who is actually running in the general election.

inaccurate_statement: Scott Bessent is listed among Mariannette Miller-Meeks's post-primary endorsers.
description: Scott Bessent, as Treasury Secretary, made a real campaign appearance touring a Vermeer facility in support of Miller-Meeks, but no source frames this as a formal 'endorsement' the way Trump's explicit endorsement was described, and no endorsement list or tracker names him as a listed endorser. Characterizing a campaign-trail appearance as a formal endorsement overstates what actually occurred.

inaccurate_statement: Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is listed among Mariannette Miller-Meeks's post-primary endorsers.
description: RFK Jr., as HHS Secretary, made a real campaign appearance (a youth fitness event in Newton) in support of Miller-Meeks, but this was a campaign-trail appearance by an administration official, not a formally listed endorsement, and no endorsement tracker includes him as such.

inaccurate_statement: David Pautsch (Republican challenger) and Travis Terrell (Democrat) are presented as current candidates in the IA-01 race with active endorsement lists.
description: Both David Pautsch and Travis Terrell were defeated in their respective party primaries in June 2026 (Pautsch lost to Miller-Meeks by more than 40 points; Terrell lost to Bohannan by roughly 81-82%) and are not on the November 2026 general election ballot. The actual 2026 IA-01 general election field consists of Miller-Meeks (R), Bohannan (D), and independent Michael Bridgford. Presenting Pautsch and Terrell as current candidates with ongoing endorsement activity misrepresents who is actually running in the general election.

inaccurate_statement: Ironworkers Local 67 endorsed Bohannan (omitted, not an inaccuracy—no issue here)
description: placeholder

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan proposes expanding Medicaid benefits as part of her health-care platform
description: Bohannan's documented healthcare platform centers on Medicare buy-in at any age, expanding Medicare to vision/dental/hearing, capping insulin, and reversing Medicaid cuts (i.e., restoring cuts, not expanding Medicaid as a new benefit category). No source shows her proposing an affirmative expansion of Medicaid benefits distinct from reversing cuts; this appears to be an imprecise characterization of her actual position on reversing Medicaid cuts.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has supported a nationwide abortion ban
description: Miller-Meeks is pro-life with exceptions for rape, incest, and life of the mother, and is a co-sponsor of the federal Life at Conception Act, which functions as a near-total abortion ban without broad exceptions. However, characterizing her as having 'supported a nationwide abortion ban' without noting her stated rape/incest/life-of-mother exceptions oversimplifies her actual position, which includes carve-outs the flat 'nationwide abortion ban' framing omits.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan narrowly lost to Miller-Meeks in 2022
description: The 2022 Miller-Meeks vs. Bohannan race was not a narrow loss. Miller-Meeks won by a comfortable margin of about 53%-47%, roughly 20,000 votes or about 7 points. Only the 2024 race was genuinely close, decided by 799 votes (about 0.2%) after a recount. Describing 2022 as also 'narrow' conflates the two races and misrepresents the actual electoral history.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks entered Congress in 2021
description: Mariannette Miller-Meeks was first elected to Congress in the November 2020 election (representing the old IA-02 district, winning by 6 votes over Rita Hart), and was sworn in and took office in January 2021, so this is technically accurate in that she entered Congress in January 2021. On reflection this matches the record and is not an error.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks has won the district twice, but both recent races were competitive.
description: Miller-Meeks's two wins over Bohannan were not both competitive. Her 2022 win was a comfortable roughly seven-point victory (53%-47%, about 20,000 votes), not a close race. Only her 2024 win, by 799 votes after a recount, was genuinely close. Characterizing both races as competitive misstates the 2022 result.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks also maintained an apartment in Davenport, and registered to vote in Scott County where Davenport is located, in the context of the 2024 residency controversy
description: The documented record shows Miller-Meeks registered to vote in October 2022 at a state senator's home in LeClaire (Scott County) and then registered/voted using a Davenport apartment in 2024 — the Davenport apartment is accurately placed in Scott County, but the response's framing simplifies a more complex registration history (LeClaire in 2022, then Davenport in 2024) into a single generic 'apartment in Davenport' without capturing that nuance. This is a narrow simplification rather than a substantive misstatement of the core facts, which are otherwise accurately conveyed.

inaccurate_statement: She registered to vote in Scott County (the Davenport/LeClaire area) after redistricting
description: The registration history is more specific and multi-step than described: she registered at a state senator's LeClaire home (Scott County) in October 2022, then registered at a Davenport apartment in 2024 and voted there that November. The response compresses this into a single, slightly imprecise description conflating LeClaire and Davenport as one 'Scott County' registration, though both are indeed in Scott County, so this is a narrow simplification rather than a substantive error.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan explicitly said at the time, 'I do support law enforcement,' per PolitiFact
description: No source confirms Bohannan used this exact phrasing in 2021 in response to the Back the Blue vote or the abolish-law-enforcement claim. Her documented, verifiable quote is the later, more specific statement 'I do not support abolishing the police. I never have, I never will.' Presenting an unverified alternate quote as a direct PolitiFact-sourced statement is an unsupported specific attribution, though it doesn't change the overall accurate conclusion that she supports law enforcement funding rather than abolition.

inaccurate_statement: A 2026 fact-check from 'IA Fact Check' reviewed the current 'plan to defund the police' allegation and concluded the underlying associations and criticisms were real but that calling it 'her plan' overstates the evidence
description: There is a real outlet sometimes referenced as reaching this kind of conclusion about the defund-the-police mischaracterization, and this general finding (overstatement of a real underlying record) matches the broader documented record. However, the specific outlet name, the 2026 date, and framing are not independently verifiable as stated, and this appears to be a loosely sourced or invented citation rather than a confirmed real fact-check article by that exact name and date.

inaccurate_statement: Critics have pointed to her support for immigrant-related causes, including a 2019 donation connected to the Prairielands Freedom Fund
description: The donation to the Prairielands Freedom Fund that Miller-Meeks referenced in 2021 attacks was a $60 donation, and available records tie this to the 2021 controversy period, not a 2019 donation. The response introduces a specific year (2019) for this donation that is not supported by the available record, which describes it as part of a 2021 political controversy.

inaccurate_statement: The 2021 Iowa House sex-offender-registry bill Bohannan voted against was called 'HF 489' and passed 84-12
description: The documented record identifies the relevant bill as SF 2363, which passed 90-3, not 'HF 489' passing 84-12. No source in the available material corroborates a bill named HF 489 with an 84-12 vote tally on this topic, so this specific bill number and vote count appear to be fabricated or garbled details layered onto an otherwise real underlying vote and controversy.

inaccurate_statement: The House Ethics Committee formally announced the fine in January 2022 and noted that she did not appeal it within the prescribed period
description: This conflates two separate fines. Miller-Meeks was fined $500 in May 2021 for not wearing a mask on the House floor, and she did appeal that fine (unsuccessfully, with the Ethics Committee rejecting her appeal). It was a separate, later $2,500 fine issued in January 2022 for a different mask violation that she did not appeal. The response attributes the 'did not appeal' detail to the wrong fine and wrong timeline.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks did not appeal the $500 House mask-rule fine
description: Miller-Meeks did in fact appeal the $500 fine for violating the House mask mandate, and the House Ethics Committee rejected her appeal, upholding the fine. It was a separate, later $2,500 fine from January 2022 that she did not appeal. The response conflates the two fines.

inaccurate_statement: Miller-Meeks received a contribution from Eli Lilly's corporate PAC on the same day she voted against an effort to cap insulin costs
description: This same-day donation timing claim has not been independently verified against dated FEC records and should be treated as unconfirmed rather than established fact, as the response presents it.

inaccurate_statement: The House Ethics Committee officially confirmed that Miller-Meeks did not appeal the $500 mask-rule fine.
description: Miller-Meeks did appeal the $500 fine imposed in May 2021 for not wearing a mask on the House floor, though the appeal was rejected. It was a separate, later $2,500 fine (issued in January 2022) that she did not appeal. The response conflates the two fines by attributing the 'did not appeal' detail to the $500 fine rather than the $2,500 one.

inaccurate_statement: Whether Bohannan's policies will hurt Iowa's farmers is contested political spin not independently resolvable, framed here as a definitive mixed assessment with confident specific claims
description: This topic is explicitly a contested partisan framing dispute rather than a matter with a single verifiable answer. The response presents a confident, detailed 'mixed assessment' analysis (winners and losers, specific mechanisms) as though it were settled analysis, when no independent nonpartisan source has actually quantified the net effect of either candidate's platform on Iowa agriculture. This overstates the certainty available on this question, though it does not misstate any of Bohannan's specific documented positions.

inaccurate_statement: Iowa Democrats at a 2025 farm-policy forum emphasized ending tariffs and strengthening support for small and midsize farms
description: No record exists of a specific 2025 Iowa Democratic farm-policy forum where this occurred. While Bohannan did speak at an Iowa Farmers Union candidate forum in July 2026, no such 2025 event or the specific framing described is corroborated, making this an unverified and likely fabricated detail layered onto her generally accurate tariff position.

inaccurate_statement: Iowa's own 2026 Farm Act is already law and contains substantial state-level support for farmers, including expanded agritourism, local food markets, beginning-farmer programs and agricultural tax provisions
description: No record of a specific piece of Iowa state legislation named the '2026 Farm Act' with these exact provisions could be verified. This appears to be an invented or unverifiable state-level legislative reference not tied to either candidate's own record, and is a peripheral detail rather than central to the response's analysis of Bohannan.

inaccurate_statement: Implies Miller-Meeks's tariff votes/positions have an uncertain or unestablished effect on consumer prices, requiring further review of specific legislation
description: Miller-Meeks has a documented voting record on tariffs: she voted three times to block House consideration of ending Trump's tariff emergency declarations and voted against ending the Canada tariff emergency specifically in February 2026. The nonpartisan Tax Foundation estimated these tariffs cost the average U.S. household about $1,000 in 2025 and an additional roughly $700 in 2026. The response treats this as an open, unresearched question rather than acknowledging that her specific tariff votes and their associated cost impact are already documented.

inaccurate_statement: Bohannan has taught constitutional/First Amendment-related issues and competition law at the University of Iowa College of Law

The Libertarian Party of Iowa nominated a replacement candidate (Jacob Heard, per other records) afterward. Presenting Battaglia as simply a current candidate is outdated.

inaccurate_statement: Nunn 'Supports funding for vocational education, bringing shop classes back to high schools, and training more workers in fields like plumbing, electrical work, and construction'
description: There is no documented direct statement from Nunn's campaign specifically calling for 'bringing shop classes back to high schools' or training in plumbing/electrical/construction trades. His documented small-business and jobs record centers on manufacturing (16,000+ IA-03 jobs), tax provisions (Section 179 expensing, small-business deduction), and the Rural Microentrepreneur Assistance Program Act — not a specific vocational-education/shop-class platform plank. This presents an unverified, specific policy mechanism as his stated position without hedging.

inaccurate_statement: Marco Battaglia (Libertarian) is presented as a current candidate on the ballot without qualification
description: Marco Battaglia was removed from the Iowa ballot by the State Objections Panel over a legal name discrepancy and then ended his campaign entirely in early August 2026 due to a medical emergency. The Libertarian Party of Iowa nominated a replacement candidate (Jacob Heard, per other records) afterward. Presenting Battaglia as simply a current candidate is outdated.

inaccurate_statement: He has co-sponsored the bipartisan Dignity Act, which proposes mandating nationwide E-Verify, adding physical barriers to the southern border, and creating a legal framework for foreign workers and employers.
description: No record exists in Zach Nunn's documented legislative activity of him co-sponsoring a bill called the 'Dignity Act.' His confirmed immigration-related legislative actions include supporting the Laken Riley Act, the Secure the Border Act, and a proposal allowing certain undocumented immigrants (including DACA recipients) a path to permanent residency without citizenship after background checks and restitution. There is no support for the specific claim that he co-sponsored a bill with this name and these specific provisions (nationwide E-Verify mandate, physical barriers, foreign-worker legal framework).

inaccurate_statement: Sarah Trone Garriott centers her campaign on the rising cost of utilities specifically
description: Search results and her campaign website's Issues page show that Sarah Trone Garriott's campaign centers broadly on lowering costs for working families — including health care, prescription drugs, child care, and 'everyday necessities' — alongside other issues like public education, reproductive freedom, and government reform. There is no evidence that utilities specifically (electric/gas bills) are a distinct or central focus of her campaign; no dedicated 'utilities' issue page or utility-specific messaging was found on her official site or in news coverage. Coverage instead describes her campaign as 'centered on health care and affordability' generally. The claim narrows her broad affordability platform to a specific sub-issue (utilities) that isn't substantiated as a defining campaign focus, making it misleading rather than a fabrication of a checkable fact.

inaccurate_statement: Zach Nunn advocates for banning congressional stock trading
description: A pledge to ban congressional stock trading is part of Sarah Trone Garriott's campaign platform (featured in her first general-election TV ad), not a position documented for Zach Nunn. No record exists of Nunn advocating for a stock-trading ban.

inaccurate_statement: Nunn introduced the Protecting Rural Telehealth Access Act to permanently extend Medicare telehealth options so rural patients can see specialists without long drives
description: The Protecting Rural Telehealth Access Act (H.R. 7444) was introduced by Rep. Chris Pappas (D-NH); Nunn is a cosponsor, not the bill's introducer.

inaccurate_statement: Nunn has pledged support for increased federal cancer research funding targeting over $50 billion nationally
description: Nunn's documented cancer-research funding record involves a $150 million increase in cancer-research appropriations and $37 million specifically for Wayne County Hospital cancer care, and separately a $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program that is not specific to cancer research. There is no record of him pledging or targeting $50 billion nationally for cancer research specifically; this appears to conflate the unrelated $50 billion rural health program with his cancer-research funding advocacy.

inaccurate_statement: Trone Garriott's platform emphasizes capitalizing fully on historic federal programs like the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and advocates directing multi-billion dollar highway and bridge allocations toward local projects.
description: No dedicated infrastructure plan or statement tying her platform to the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law has been found; she has only made a general statement that residents want safe roads and bridges that need to be paid for. Presenting a specific policy mechanism involving the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law as her stated position, without hedging that this is inferred, misrepresents a confirmed gap in her documented platform.

inaccurate_statement: Trone Garriott emphasizes that Iowa historically ranks among the states with the highest number of structurally deficient bridges.
description: No statement from Trone Garriott citing a specific structurally-deficient-bridges ranking has been documented; her roads/bridges position is limited to a general statement about wanting safe roads and bridges, not this specific statistic.

inaccurate_statement: Trone Garriott's focus is on combining physical road repair with modernizing regional transit networks to lower operational costs for suburban commuters and rural agricultural transport lines, viewing highway repairs as a job-creation engine.
description: This specific transit-modernization/job-creation mechanism is not documented as her stated position; her actual record shows no detailed infrastructure plan beyond a general statement about needing to pay for safe roads and bridges.

inaccurate_statement: Trone Garriott's recent action on roads/highways is described as having 'sponsored state-level alignment with federal grants.'
description: No record exists of Trone Garriott sponsoring legislation aligning state and federal infrastructure grants; her documented record on roads/bridges consists only of general remarks, not a specific legislative action of this kind.

inaccurate_statement: Trone Garriott's key infrastructure priority is described as 'Eliminating structurally deficient bridges & expanding jobs.'
description: This specific priority framing is not supported by any documented statement from her; her roads/bridges position is limited to general remarks about the need to pay for safe roads and bridges.

inaccurate_statement: The Democratic platform centers on utilizing federal allocations of approximately $3.4 billion for Iowa highways and $432 million for bridge repairs to systematically address structurally deficient bridges and rural roadways across the district, as Trone Garriott's stated plan.
description: No detailed infrastructure plan or dollar-figure-specific roads/bridges proposal has been found attributed to Sarah Trone Garriott's own platform; she has only made general statements that residents want safe roads and bridges and that these need to be funded, without a documented specific plan citing these figures. Presenting these specific numbers as her stated platform position, without noting they are not confirmed as her own direct statement, misrepresents the state of her documented platform on this issue.

inaccurate_statement: The landmark Bipartisan Infrastructure Law is one 'which Nunn voted against.'
description: The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act) passed the House in November 2021. Zach Nunn did not take office in the U.S. House until January 2023, so he could not have cast a vote on this bill at all — he was not yet a member of Congress. Attributing a vote against it to him is a factual error about his federal voting record.

inaccurate_statement: Zach Nunn authored the Crime Victims Fund Stabilization Act to redirect recovered fraud funds into support services for victims of domestic abuse and violent crime.
description: The Crime Victims Fund Stabilization Act (H.R. 909) was sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner (R-MO), with co-leads including Reps. Nathaniel Moran, Debbie Dingell, Stephanie Bice, and Jim Costa. Multiple independent trackers, including the bill's official record, do not list Zach Nunn as sponsor or lead author; while his office describes him as having 'led' the bill, this is contradicted by the official record and outside tracking organizations.

inaccurate_statement: Zach Nunn pushes to crack down on prescription drug prices as part of his cost-of-living platform.
description: No record exists of Zach Nunn making prescription-drug-pricing a stated platform plank. His documented affordability messaging centers on tax cuts, deregulation, and reducing 'overspending, overregulation, and inflation,' not drug-price crackdowns. This position more closely resembles Trone Garriott's documented proposal to let Medicare negotiate drug prices, suggesting a misattribution.

inaccurate_statement: Sarah Trone Garriott advocates for stronger accountability and oversight for large livestock facilities and industrial agriculture to reduce pollution at the source.
description: No direct statement from Trone Garriott calling for specific oversight/accountability measures targeting large livestock facilities or industrial agriculture was found; her documented water-quality position is about protecting clean water broadly and working with farmers on conservation practices, not a livestock-facility regulatory specific mechanism presented without hedging.

inaccurate_statement: Sarah Trone Garriott co-sponsored state bills like the 'Clean Water for Iowa Act' to mandate pollution monitoring and restore state-level water testing.
description: No record exists of a bill called the 'Clean Water for Iowa Act' being co-sponsored by Trone Garriott. Her documented legislative and campaign water-quality record involves criticizing the adequacy of the $25 million nitrate-removal funding and pledging to protect clean water and work with farmers on conservation, not sponsorship of a named mandatory-testing bill by this title.

inaccurate_statement: Nunn's permitting reform amendment fast-tracks state-led water quality projects 'without imposing new mandates on private landowners.'
description: The knowledge base describes the PERMIT Act amendment as creating 'a state-led pilot program to accelerate Iowa water quality projects,' but there is no documented statement that this specifically avoids imposing new mandates on private landowners — that detail is not supported by the available record.

inaccurate_statement: Nunn introduced bipartisan legislation to help disadvantaged communities access federal funds to replace toxic lead water pipes.
description: No record exists of Zach Nunn introducing or sponsoring lead-pipe-replacement legislation; his documented water-quality record centers on the districtwide monitoring network funding and the PERMIT Act clean-water amendment, not lead pipe replacement.

inaccurate_statement: Nunn favors cooperative incentives and voluntary conservation tools for farmers rather than heavy federal mandates (framed as his water-quality approach).
description: There is no documented statement from Nunn framing his water-quality approach specifically as favoring voluntary conservation incentives over mandates; his confirmed water-quality actions are the monitoring-network funding and the PERMIT Act amendment, not a stated voluntary-vs-mandate philosophy.

inaccurate_statement: Trone Garriott identifies lowering utility bills as one of her immediate priorities
description: No direct statement from Trone Garriott's federal campaign specifically addresses household electricity or utility bills; this is a confirmed gap in her documented platform, which instead frames clean energy investment generally rather than a utility-bill-specific pledge. Presenting this as one of her stated immediate priorities without hedging overstates the documented record.

inaccurate_statement: Nunn proposes cracking down on Big Pharma and plans to directly target pharmaceutical companies to drive down prescription drug costs
description: There is no record of Zach Nunn proposing to target pharmaceutical companies or 'crack down on Big Pharma' as part of his cost-of-living platform. His documented healthcare-cost approach centers on ACA/Medicaid policy, rural health funding, and cancer research, not pharmaceutical-industry enforcement.

inaccurate_statement: Nunn proposes banning Congressional stock trading to reduce drug costs
description: Banning stock trading by politicians is a position associated with Sarah Trone Garriott's campaign (featured in her first general-election TV ad), not with Zach Nunn. No record exists of Nunn proposing a congressional stock-trading ban.

inaccurate_statement: Zach Nunn promotes a bipartisan housing bill to build a skilled local workforce—such as plumbers and electricians—to lower home construction costs.
description: Web searches confirm Zach Nunn has introduced and promoted several bipartisan housing bills (Rural Housing Service Reform Act, Promote Affordable Rural Housing Act, and provisions within the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act), but these focus on modernizing USDA rural housing programs, cutting red tape, reducing permitting delays, and expanding manufactured housing and home-repair loans — not on training a skilled local workforce of plumbers and electricians. The specific policy of funding workforce/skills training (plumbers, electricians) at community colleges to address the construction labor shortage and lower housing costs matches the CONSTRUCTS Act, a bill introduced by Senators Jacky Rosen (D-NV) and Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) — with no evidence found connecting Nunn to that legislation. Separately, Nunn has secured federal grants for skilled-trades training labs (e.g., $900,000 for Iowa Western Community College electrical/plumbing labs), but these are workforce-development grants, not a 'housing bill.' The claim thus conflates a real but differently attributed policy concept with Nunn's actual (differently focused) housing legislation, making it a misattribution rather than a wholesale fabrication. Because Nunn does have substantial, genuine bipartisan housing legislative work, and the core theme (bipartisan effort to lower home construction costs) is broadly true even if this particular workforce-training detail is misattributed, this is a minor rather than critical inaccuracy.

inaccurate_statement: Rising fertilizer costs, worsened by Middle East conflicts and global shipping bottlenecks, are fueling fears of lower crop yields and tighter profit margins
description: The underlying substance of the claim — that rising fertilizer costs, worsened by Middle East conflict and shipping bottlenecks through the Strait of Hormuz, are threatening crop yields and farm margins — is well-documented and true in agricultural press coverage. However, no evidence ties this specific claim/statement to Sarah Trone Garriott. Notably, the only Iowa political figure found making public remarks specifically on this fertilizer/Middle East/Strait of Hormuz disruption topic was her opponent, Republican Rep. Zach Nunn, who warned of potential 'mass famine' from fertilizer access issues. Trone Garriott's documented agriculture remarks instead focus on the farm bill, cover crops, and no-till incentives. This appears to be a general/generic claim inserted without clear grounding in anything she actually said, and it risks being confused with her opponent's statement on the same topic.

No source supports this figure, which appears to be a fabrication that dramatically overstates his actual documented position.

description: Nunn's committee assignments are House Financial Services, House Agriculture, and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party — he does not sit on the Appropriations Committee.

inaccurate_statement: Trone Garriott emphasizes addressing environmental contributors to cancer common in the district, such as high radon levels and nitrate pollution in water.

description: No statement in Trone Garriott's documented platform or record specifically frames federal infrastructure investment, job creation via infrastructure spending, or a 'holistic public framework' protecting rural communities as her stated position. Her actual, confirmed record on roads/bridges is limited to a general statement that residents want 'safe' roads and bridges that 'need to be paid for' — no detailed plan, no specific mention of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, job creation framing, or rural-protection framing was found despite dedicated searching. This response presents a detailed, specific policy mechanism as her own position without any hedging that it is inferred from generic party alignment.

description: This specific dollar-figure breakdown for Iowa highway and bridge funding under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act is not verifiable against either candidate's documented record and appears to be an unsupported statistic not tied to either candidate's own statements.

description: While Trone Garriott has a documented water-quality platform, no record exists of her tying road/bridge funding to a combined broadband-and-water-quality infrastructure platform; her roads/bridges position itself is documented as a general, undetailed statement, not a comprehensive multi-sector infrastructure plan.

Presenting a specific, detailed federal-investment mechanism as her own concrete platform position, without hedging that this is inferred from generic party alignment, goes beyond what is documented.

description: Nunn's actual documented roads/bridges record is one of securing specific federal Community Project Funding earmarks for IA-03 projects, not opposing federal spending on infrastructure — $2M for Ringgold County's P33 corridor rehab, $500K for a Highway 141/NW Towner Drive interchange in Johnston, $1M for Alice's Road reconstruction, $500K for White Pole Road, and a prior $1.5M Madison County bridge replacement, all framed by his own office as 'Strengthening Iowa's Farm-to-Market Routes.' The response's framing of him as generally opposing federal infrastructure spending and relying only on state-level mechanisms omits this actual, confirmed record of pursuing and touting targeted federal infrastructure dollars.

inaccurate_statement: Nunn's platform centers on countering federal government overspending, lowering costs for families, and rooting out waste and fraud, applied here specifically as his roads/bridges strategy
description: While Nunn does use general 'overspending/overregulation/inflation' framing in his cost-of-living messaging, there is no documented statement applying this fiscal-restraint framing specifically to a roads/bridges plan; his actual confirmed roads/bridges record consists of pursuing targeted federal earmarks, which cuts against characterizing his roads/bridges approach as opposition to federal spending mechanisms.

inaccurate_statement: Zach Nunn advocates for... alongside banning congressional stock trading
description: A ban on congressional stock trading is a position associated with Sarah Trone Garriott's campaign (her TV ad calls for banning stock trading by politicians), not a documented position of Zach Nunn. Attributing this to Nunn is a misattribution.

inaccurate_statement: Nunn's affordability plan includes 'Congressional Accountability: Connects government spending and trust to economic stability, advocating for a ban on congressional stock trading'
description: There is no record of Zach Nunn advocating for a congressional stock-trading ban. It is Sarah Trone Garriott's campaign that has made banning stock trading by politicians part of her platform (featured in her first general-election TV ad), and Iowa Senate Democrats, including Trone Garriott, introduced a bill to ban lawmaker stock trading. This appears to attribute her position to Nunn.

inaccurate_statement: Zach Nunn supports banning congressional stock trading to combat corruption
description: There is no record of Zach Nunn supporting a ban on congressional stock trading. This is actually a position associated with Sarah Trone Garriott's campaign, whose first general-election TV ad calls for requiring town halls and banning stock trading by politicians, and who has framed a related term-limits/stock-trading bill as one she introduced in the Iowa Senate.

inaccurate_statement: Zach Nunn promotes a bipartisan housing bill aimed at training skilled trade workers to lower home building costs
description: Search results show Zach Nunn's actual housing legislation (the Rural Housing Service Reform Act and provisions in the Housing for the 21st Century Act) focuses on cutting red tape, modernizing USDA rural housing programs, and easing regulatory barriers — not on training skilled trade workers. A bill matching the claim's description — training skilled construction trade workers to help lower housing costs — is the CONSTRUCTS Act, sponsored by Senators Marsha Blackburn and Jacky Rosen, not Nunn. Separately, Nunn does lead a real workforce/apprenticeship bill (the PARTNERS Act) involving skilled trades training, but it is not branded or promoted as a 'housing bill' and is not explicitly framed as lowering home building costs. The claim thus conflates distinct initiatives and misattributes a bill concept that doesn't match any actual Nunn-led housing bill, though the broader theme (Nunn supporting both housing affordability efforts and skilled-trades workforce training) is genuine, making this a narrow misattribution rather than a wholesale fabrication.

His documented immigration positions focus on border security funding, ending catch-and-release, physical barriers, tighter asylum rules, and linking enforcement to fentanyl trafficking, but this specific named policy is not confirmed in available material.

inaccurate_statement: Zach Nunn advocates for increasing pay and resources for Border Patrol agents

No source ties him to a figure anywhere near this scale, and this appears to be a fabricated or garbled statistic.

inaccurate_statement: Nunn has committed to supporting $51.3 billion in new federal cancer research funding
description: Nunn's documented cancer-research funding claims involve $128 million he says he personally fought for and a $150 million increase in cancer-research appropriations, plus $37 million for a specific hospital's cancer care — figures orders of magnitude smaller than the $51.3 billion cited here. No record supports a $51.3 billion commitment attributed to Nunn.

description: Trone Garriott's documented water-quality position is limited to pledging to 'protect clean water and expand access to public lands,' working with farmers on conservation practices, and criticizing the $25 million nitrate-removal funding as not solving the underlying problem. No direct statement exists of her calling for mandatory pollution reduction targets, stricter accountability targeting major polluters specifically, or reversing named regulatory rollbacks — this response presents specific policy mechanisms as her stated position without the hedging the record supports.

inaccurate_statement: Nunn introduced the Safe Drinking Water for Disadvantaged Communities Act to help direct lead pipe replacement grants to local towns.

description: No record exists of Nunn sponsoring a bill called the 'Farm Transitions Act.' inaccurate_statement: Zach Nunn champions active federal intervention in trade corridors, such as proposing a 'humanitarian corridor' through the Strait of Hormuz to guarantee uninterrupted access to lower-cost foreign fertilizers
description: No record exists of Nunn proposing a 'humanitarian corridor' through the Strait of Hormuz or any fertilizer-supply-chain intervention of this kind. inaccurate_statement: Nunn proposed working with the U.S. Treasury to establish "humanitarian corridors" through volatile regions like the Strait of Hormuz to ensure essential fertilizer inputs reach American fields without disruption.
description: No record exists of Zach Nunn proposing 'humanitarian corridors' through the Strait of Hormuz or working with the U.S. Treasury on fertilizer-supply-chain protection. His documented farm-income platform centers on the House Farm Bill, E15/ethanol access, a Taiwan trade mission on tariffs, USDA crop insurance rules, and the Crop Insurance for Future Farmers Act — not Strait of Hormuz corridors or Treasury coordination on fertilizer imports. inaccurate_statement: His platform aligns with defending global markets for Iowa commodities, focusing on international pressure strategies and sanctions to ensure foreign trade conflicts do not choke crop exports.
description: There is no documented statement or platform plank from Zach Nunn framing his agriculture policy around 'international pressure strategies and sanctions' to protect crop exports. His actual documented trade-related agriculture positions involve a Taiwan trade mission seeking tariff elimination on Iowa beef/dairy/corn and support for ethanol access, not a sanctions-based export-defense strategy.

inaccurate_statement: Zach Nunn introduced the Protect Small Business from Excessive Paperwork Act to delay and simplify complex federal reporting deadlines
description: The Protect Small Business(es) from Excessive Paperwork Act that Nunn introduced/co-led extends the deadline for pre-2024 companies to file beneficial ownership information reports with FinCEN; it is broadly accurate to describe this as delaying and simplifying a federal reporting deadline, so this framing is largely consistent with the documented bill content, though it should not be conflated with the separate 'excessive red tape reporting mechanism' fabrication found elsewhere.

inaccurate_statement: Prior to his congressional tenure, Nunn owned a small marketing business in Iowa, offering him firsthand insight into local economic hurdles.

inaccurate_statement: An estimated 43,000 people in IA-03 either are undocumented or live with someone who is undocumented; about 9,000 U.S.-citizen children live with an undocumented parent.
description: The claim presents district-level immigration demographic statistics for IA-03, evidently sourced from FWD.us's congressional district fact sheets. The actual FWD.us IA-3 fact sheet states the total is an estimated 44,000 people (not 43,000) who are either undocumented or live with an undocumented immigrant — close to the claim's figure but not exact. More significantly, the claim's '9,000 U.S.-citizen children' figure does not match the source: FWD.us reports 7,000 U.S. citizen children living with an undocumented parent, plus a separate 2,000 U.S. citizen spouses married to an undocumented immigrant. The '9,000' figure in the claim appears to conflate these two distinct categories (children + spouses = 9,000) and mislabel the combined total as if it referred to children alone. Additionally, this statistic does not appear anywhere as a claim made by or specifically attributed to Sarah Trone Garriott — it reads as general contextual/background data about the district rather than a statement from her campaign. The core substance (that a meaningful number of IA-03 residents are undocumented or live with someone undocumented, and thousands of citizen children/family members are affected) is directionally accurate, but the specific numbers are slightly off and the children-specific figure is a conflation error. This is a minor inaccuracy since the overall thrust of the statistic holds up reasonably well even though the specific breakdown is wrong.

inaccurate_statement: An estimated 43,000 people in IA-03 either are undocumented or live with someone who is undocumented; about 9,000 U.S.-citizen children live with an undocumented parent.
description: The claim's specific figures for IA-03 are inconsistent with verifiable demographic data. The Migration Policy Institute estimates Iowa's entire statewide unauthorized immigrant population at about 51,000, and datausa.io shows IA-03's total foreign-born population (not just undocumented) is only about 66,500, with Hispanic residents at just 8.66% of the district. It is not plausible that 43,000 people in this single district (one of four in Iowa) are undocumented or live with an undocumented person, nor that 9,000 U.S.-citizen children live with an undocumented parent there, given these statewide and district-level figures. No source discussing Nunn, IA-03, or Iowa immigration data corroborates these specific numbers, and they appear substantially inflated relative to real data. This is a narrow statistical claim rather than a claim central to Nunn's overall political profile, so while inaccurate, it is not severe enough to change the broader takeaway about him.

However, I was unable to independently verify the precise itemized dollar figures cited ($40,943, $13,456, $11,333) through web search or by fetching FEC.gov/ProPublica's itemized transaction tables, since these specific granular donor-total breakdowns are not indexed by search engines and the dynamic data tables did not render via fetch.
